# Introduction to DOM

#### Course: JavaScript in Browser

## Introduction to DOM

When you open a webpage, the browser organizes the HTML document into a tree-like model. For example,

```html
1<!DOCTYPE html>
2<html lang="en">
3
4    <head>
5        <title>Price List</title>
6    </head>
7
8    <body>
9        <div class="container">
10            <h1>Price List</h1>
11            <ul id="price-list">
12                <li class="item">Milk <span>$2.50</span></li>
13                <li class="item">Bread <span>$1.50</span></li>
14                <li class="item">Toothpaste <span>$3.00</span></li>
15            </ul>
16        </div>
17    </body>
18    
19</html>
```

```css
1* {
2    margin: 0;
3    padding: 0;
4    box-sizing: border-box;
5}
6
7body {
8    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
9    display: flex;
10    justify-content: center;
11    background-color: #f5f5f5;
12}
13
14.container {
15    width: 100%;
16    max-width: 400px;
17}
18h1 {
19    color: #1a237e;
20    font-size: 24px;
21    margin: 16px;
22}
23
24#price-list {
25    background-color: white;
26    border: 1px solid #e0e0e0;
27    border-radius: 8px;
28}
29
30.item {
31    padding: 12px;
32    font-size: 18px;
33    color: #1a237e;
34    border-top: 1px solid #ddd;
35    display: flex;
36    justify-content: space-between;
37
38}
39
40.item:first-child {
41    border-top: none;
42}
```

The above code is processed by the browser as shown below:

![Introduction](data:image/png;base64,)

This is the DOM tree.

While the image above simplifies by showing only HTML elements, the full DOM tree includes elements, attributes, and text—such as "Price List" inside the <h1> and "Milk" inside the <div>.
